summary: Reviewed the dvpwa (Damn Vulnerable Python Web Application) aiohttp project: DAO layer, views, routes, auth utilities, middlewares, Jinja2 setup, templates and configuration. The application is intentionally insecure and contains an unauthenticated SQL injection, stored XSS (global autoescape disabled), disabled CSRF protection, weak unsalted MD5 password hashing, and JavaScript-accessible session cookies. Overall risk is critical: an unauthenticated remote attacker can inject SQL and persistently inject scripts. Coverage is the full Python source and templates; static vendored JS/CSS and font assets were not reviewed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: The INSERT query is built with Python %-string formatting of the attacker-supplied student name instead of a parameterized query. The value flows unvalidated from the unauthenticated POST /students/ handler (views.py:54-57, data['name'], no schema check) directly into the SQL string. An attacker can submit a name like `x'); DROP TABLE students; --` or use stacked/sub-queries to read or modify arbitrary data. Reachable by any anonymous user. Note: every other DAO method (student.py:18, course.py, review.py, mark.py, user.py) correctly uses bound parameters; this is the single string-formatted sink.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  -> cur.execute(q)  ; source: views.students POST -> Student.create(conn, data['name'])
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Also enforce STUDENT_SCHEMA on the input in the view.

findings.title: Stored XSS via globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled, persisted data is rendered raw, producing stored XSS. The clearest reachable path: the unauthenticated POST /courses/{id}/review handler (views.py:111-131) stores review_text verbatim, which course.jinja2:22 renders as `{{ review.review_text }}`. Any visitor to the course page then executes attacker JavaScript. The same disabled escaping also makes course.title/description, student.name, and user names injectable sinks across the templates. Combined with the httponly=False session cookie this yields session theft/account takeover.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)  ; sink: templates/course.jinja2:22 `{{ review.review_text }}` ; source: views.review POST -> Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text)
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=select_autoescape(['jinja2','html']) or True) and explicitly mark only known-safe output. Do not rely on per-template escaping with it globally off.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled application-wide
findings.description: A working CSRF middleware exists (middlewares.py:25-38) and templates emit a _csrf_token, but the middleware is commented out of the middleware chain, so no POST request's token is ever validated. All state-changing endpoints (POST /, /students/, /courses/, /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id}, /courses/{id}/review, /logout/) accept forged cross-site requests. Because the session cookie is used ambiently, an attacker page can create students, courses, reviews, assign marks, or log the victim out on their behalf.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]  (csrf_middleware is commented out despite being implemented in middlewares.py:25-38)
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list (and ensure token generation runs for GET forms), or use a maintained CSRF library.

findings.title: Unsalted MD5 used for password hashing
findings.description: Password verification compares the stored hash to a plain, unsalted MD5 of the supplied password; fixtures also seed pwd_hash with md5() (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13). MD5 is fast and unsalted, so any disclosed users.pwd_hash column (e.g. via the SQL injection above) is trivially cracked with rainbow tables/brute force, and identical passwords yield identical hashes. The comparison is also non-constant-time.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  ; fixtures: VALUES ('Super',...,md5('superadmin'),TRUE), ... md5('password') ...
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt/argon2/scrypt via passlib) and compare with the library's verify (constant-time). Migrate existing hashes.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: RedisStorage is created with httponly=False, so the session identifier cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Together with the stored XSS from disabled autoescaping, an attacker can exfiltrate the session cookie via document.cookie and hijack authenticated (including admin) sessions. The cookie is also not marked Secure, allowing transmission over plain HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default) and set secure=True so the session cookie is inaccessible to JS and only sent over HTTPS.

findings.title: aiohttp application started with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True (and run.py sets logging to DEBUG). Debug mode increases verbosity and can surface internal details/warnings, which aids attackers in reconnaissance. This should never be enabled in production.
findings.recommendation: Disable debug (or drive it from configuration/environment so it defaults to False in production).
